body:
Apologies, I should have dropped a PR comment explaining this.

So I spent a bit of time considering this option and decided that it had the potential to be a bit of a footgun. As I understand it there's currently only one shell which supports logical paths (PowerShell) and I found that it was very easy to get "stuck" in a virtual path... here's an example of what I mean in GIF form:

![use_logical_path_false_behavior](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/918952/104112236-23063d80-5351-11eb-876d-9b93997fc179.gif)

This isn't an issue with escaping characters in PowerShell code, but rather in the way PS generates the [C++ command-line argument string](https://docs.microsoft.com/en-us/previous-versions//17w5ykft(v=vs.85)?redirectedfrom=MSDN) when it invokes an external program. There seems to be issues in the routine it uses to do this.

In the documentation I linked above, note the final three rules:
- Backslashes are interpreted literally, unless they immediately precede a double quotation mark.
- If an even number of backslashes is followed by a double quotation mark, one backslash is placed in the argv array for every pair of backslashes, and the double quotation mark is interpreted as a string delimiter.
- If an odd number of backslashes is followed by a double quotation mark, one backslash is placed in the argv array for every pair of backslashes, and the double quotation mark is "escaped" by the remaining backslash, causing a literal double quotation mark (") to be placed in argv.

E.g. for the following external command invocation:
```powershell
> $a = 'hello "world" goodbye "moon"'
> $b = 'path\without\whitespace\'
> $c = 'path\with whitespace\'
> externalprogram $a $b $c
```
PS generates the following command-line string:
```cmd
externalprogram "hello "world" goodbye "moon"" path\without\whitespace\ "path\with whitespace\"
```

The first argument is quoted incorrectly as the quote marks are not escaped. ❌
The second argument is not quoted at all as it does not contain any whitespace. ✔️ 
The third argument however has whitespace _and_ a trailing, odd number of backslashes which ends up escaping the closing quote mark. ❌

PowerShell could handle this by detecting a trailing backslash and escaping it as part of the quoted command-line string serialisation, but for some reason it doesn't. It could also trivially escape quote marks in the string. This seems an obvious oversight honestly, it's very surprising.

~I'm using PowerShell 5.0 - I haven't tested with the cross-platform PowerShell version yet so maybe they've fixed it there.~
**Edit:** There's a _four year old_ open issue on this problem: https://github.com/PowerShell/PowerShell/issues/1995

In reading through that PowerShell issue thread I learnt about the the [stop-parsing symbol (`--%`)](https://docs.microsoft.com/en-us/powershell/module/microsoft.powershell.core/about/about_parsing?view=powershell-7.1). This was introduced in PowerShell 3.0 (released in 2012) so I think we can rely on it being available.

With the stop-parsing symbol, we can manually construct a command string which we know will be correctly parsed and PS will pass it unchanged to the new process.

I've been experimenting with an `Invoke-Native` function over here:
https://github.com/deadalusai/printargs/blob/master/test.ps1

This function works around the argument escaping issue by quoting/escaping arguments manually and using `--%` to pass the argument string through to the rust executable directly. The string is quoted using the ~Windows~ C++ command-line argument string rules, and the code _appears_ to work on Linux (Ubuntu/Mint) correctly too.

Ok, it works correctly on Linux/Unix because the Unix .NET runtime itself [parses the argument string into the `argv` collection](https://github.com/dotnet/runtime/blob/9c41693194e3b005c91ee471ab3e649d2479d34d/src/libraries/System.Diagnostics.Process/src/System/Diagnostics/Process.Unix.cs#L430) before forking the new process, so we don't need to rely on distro-specific "command string to argv" parsing behavior.

["This follows the rules outlined in "Parsing C++ Command-Line Arguments" at https://msdn.microsoft.com/en-us/library/17w5ykft.aspx."](https://github.com/dotnet/runtime/blob/9c41693194e3b005c91ee471ab3e649d2479d34d/src/libraries/System.Diagnostics.Process/src/System/Diagnostics/Process.Unix.cs#L786-L789).

I've updated the PR with a more robust solution for invoking native executables (`Invoke-Native`) which ensures that the strings passed as arguments make their way into the Rust argv list in the same shape as they started, trailing backslashes and all.

You can directly strip the prefix with something like this:

```suggestion
        path.strip_prefix(r"\\?\").unwrap_or(path).to_path_buf()
```
Some paths (SMB) also have a longer prefix: `\\?\UNC\server\share`, which should be `\\server\share`. I guess this means you might not be able to use my suggestion from above.
You could prevent these clones with `std::borrow::Cow`, but I'm not sure it's worth the effort to implement here to be honest.
Actually I was thinking of always canonicalizing `context.current_dir` in `context` (at least on windows, so starship on windows supports long paths).
Please update the `directory` docs for `use_logical_path` in `docs/config/README.md` with the new behavior.

That's much simpler than what I was doing 🤦 
According to https://docs.microsoft.com/en-us/windows/win32/fileio/maximum-file-path-limitation there are only two variations of the extended path prefix, so I'll just attempt to strip them both.
Hmm, `strip_prefix` doesn't appear to work with extended path prefixes - something to do with how the path components are calculated.
I've worked around this issue by doing the extended-path prefix stripping later in the process.
No longer an issue after the `Context.current_dir`/`Context.logical_dir` refactor.

Ok, so I've run with this suggestion and made the following changes:

- `Context::current_dir` is now initialised from `--path` or `std::env::current_dir`
- Additionally `current_dir` is now always canonicalized (on *nix and windows), which expands symlinks.
   On Windows, this means that `current_dir` is now always using extended-path prefixes.
- `Context::logical_dir` is now initialised from `--logical-path` or `PWD` or `current_dir` (before canonicalization)

The `directory::module` routine now just picks between rendering `current_dir` and `logical_dir` depending on the `use_logical_dir` config setting.

+use std::ffi::OsStr;
+use std::path::{Component, Path, Prefix};
+
+#[derive(Debug, PartialEq, Eq)]
+enum NormalizedPrefix<'a> {
+    // No prefix, e.g. `\cat_pics` or `/cat_pics`
+    None,
+    /// Simple verbatim prefix, e.g. `\\?\cat_pics`.
+    Verbatim(&'a OsStr),
+    /// Device namespace prefix, e.g. `\\.\COM42`.
+    DeviceNS(&'a OsStr),
+    /// Prefix using Windows' _**U**niform **N**aming **C**onvention_, e.g. `\\server\share` or `\\?\UNC\server\share`
+    UNC(&'a OsStr, &'a OsStr),
+    /// Windows disk/drive prefix e.g. `C:` or `\\?\C:`
+    Disk(u8),
+}
+
+/// Normalise Verbatim and Non-Verbatim path prefixes into a comparable structure.
+/// NOTE: "Verbatim" paths are the rust std library's name for Windows extended-path prefixed paths.
+fn normalize_prefix(prefix: Prefix) -> NormalizedPrefix {
+    match prefix {
+        Prefix::Verbatim(segment) => NormalizedPrefix::Verbatim(segment),
+        Prefix::VerbatimUNC(server, share) => NormalizedPrefix::UNC(server, share),
+        Prefix::VerbatimDisk(disk) => NormalizedPrefix::Disk(disk),
+        Prefix::DeviceNS(device) => NormalizedPrefix::DeviceNS(device),
+        Prefix::UNC(server, share) => NormalizedPrefix::UNC(server, share),
+        Prefix::Disk(disk) => NormalizedPrefix::Disk(disk),
+    }
+}

Would you please prefix these with `starship-` or find some way to avoid getting these functions into the shell scope?

I tested your version of argument escaping, because it looks like `ArgumentList` doesn't work on PS5, but it looks like it doesn't work. Maybe try  implementing a solution based on something like https://github.com/PowerShell/PowerShell/pull/13482#issuecomment-678522514? (I'd still prefer using `ArgumentList` for PS 6.1 and up)

Because this all looks very broken without `ArgumentList` I think it might be best to just drop support for PS < 6.1 if you don't feel like doing that.

`ProcessStartInfo.ArgumentList` was only added in .NET 5.0, so this code will only work in PowerShell 6+

https://docs.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.diagnostics.processstartinfo.argumentlist?view=net-5.0&viewFallbackFrom=netframework-4.8#System_Diagnostics_ProcessStartInfo_ArgumentList

(which sucks because I'd much rather not be doing this manual escaping)

The escaping code in https://github.com/PowerShell/PowerShell/pull/13482#issuecomment-678522514 is almost identical to my escaping code, with additional complexity for unquoted arguments and batch quoting which we don't need.
I've moved these function declarations into the `global:prompt` function itself so they no longer leak into the user's shell scope.

I've adjusted the `Invoke-Native` function to use `System.Diagnostics.ProcessStartInfo` as in your suggested change above. If `ArgumentList` is available we use it, otherwise we fall back to building an escaped argument string.

Do you have any examples of argument strings which break the manual escaping process? All my test sample strings work correctly:

```powershell
$TestArguments = @(
    'hello "world" \" \\" goodbye "moon"',
    'path\without\whitespace\',
    'path\with whitespace\',
    '--flag=argument passed to flag',
    'five trailing backslashes \\\\\',
    '\\\\\five leading backslashes',
    '\\?\C:\Windows\Extended Path Syntax\',
    # Test strings from https://github.com/PowerShell/PowerShell/pull/13482
    '',
    'foo=bar none',
    '/foo:bar none',
    '-foo:bar none',
    'foo=bar "quote" none',
    'foo:not me',
    'foo=notme',
    'notmeeither',
    'c:\program files\',
    'a "b c" d',
    'a \"b c\" d',
    '3" of snow',
    'ab\',
    'a b\\',
    'a&b',
    'a"b'
);
```

When I got rid of all the `;` in `ForEach-Object` it appeared to work fine. You also might want to avoid assigning to `$_`. The VSCode PowerShell extension complains about that.
Beyond that: `ArgumentList` was added in PowerShell 6.1 with .Net Core 2.1. I think only PowerShell 7.1 has .Net 5.
